Adjoining neighbour: 4-storey building with a basement
Infill plot: the new foundation must not be above the neighbour’s foundation level, and the excavation must not endanger the existing building – excavation support may even be needed.
Old neighbour without a basement, with unknown foundations
If the new basement is deeper, the old house’s foundation has to be underpinned with concrete or strengthened with jet grouting. Its foundations have to be explored by investigation.
Protected tree at the back of the site
Restriction: no deep excavation in the root zone of the tree; the excavation and the position of the machines have to be adapted to this.
Narrow, busy street, no space for storing materials
Access to the site and how densely it is built up also affect the method: where does the concrete pump stand, where are the reinforcement and formwork stored?
Borehole: 2.4 m of made ground
Unfavourable layer: we do not found on made ground. We have to go below it to the bearing stratum, or ground improvement or another foundation type is needed.
Groundwater well: water at −2.1 m, the design level is higher
The groundwater is at basement level: dewatering, a watertight slab (inverted floor) and an uplift check all come into play.
Planned building: 6 storeys + underground car park, column frame
The size, structure and stiffness of the building decide what differential settlement it can take – a column frame can be more sensitive than a stiff wall structure.
A medical practice with sensitive equipment on the ground floor
The use also matters: equipment sensitive to vibration or settlement means stricter serviceability requirements.
Larger column loads on the street side (tower part)
Uneven load distribution causes differential settlement: larger loads need larger or stiffer foundations.
Programme: the foundations fall in January, with a tight deadline
Concreting in frost is possible only with protection; often the more expensive but faster solution wins.

We have all the data: drawings, loads, ground investigation report.
The structure, the ground and groundwater conditions, the surroundings and the site – from these we judge whether a shallow foundation can be considered.
The magnitude and position of the loads: the input for sizing the foundation area and for the stress calculation.
The structure’s sensitivity to settlement gives the acceptable displacements – the calculated settlements are compared with these.
First step: can some shallow foundation system be used? If it is clear at the very start that it cannot, we move straight on to deep foundations.
Deep foundations: a load-transferring element down to the deeper bearing stratum – later in the course.
We choose the type, then set the foundation level according to the frost depth, the bearing stratum, the groundwater, the structure and the surroundings (station 4).
We size the foundation area in the ultimate limit state: we determine the required width (for a raft it is given anyway), and make a first estimate of the depth too.
From the chosen dimensions, we calculate the stresses that develop beneath the foundation.
From the stresses we calculate the settlements, the differential settlements and the tilt.
The first “check”: are the calculated settlements and differential settlements acceptable for the planned structure?
Depth design: the depth (thickness) of the footing for load spread and strength.
Does the footing fit? If the required size does not fit (site boundary, overlapping footings, neighbour), a new foundation level or another type is needed.
Where relevant: checking the stability of position (sliding, overturning) and the safety against uplift and undermining.
Finally, the structural design of the foundation system: choosing the concrete grade and the required reinforcement.
Every check is met: the process runs straight through.
The settlement is too large: we go back – another type (e.g. stiffer, a raft), a deeper foundation level or a larger foundation area. In the second round it is met.
The required footing does not fit (e.g. because of the site boundary or overlapping footings): we set a new foundation level, or switch to a continuous raft.
It is clear at the very start of the design that a shallow foundation is out of the question: we move straight on to deep foundations.

Wrong: the new footing is above the foundation level of the old building. Its load spreads towards the old footing and loads the old wall from the side and from above; the old building may settle and crack. The new footing has to be taken down at least to the old foundation level.
Correct: the foundation level of the new building is the same as the old one. This is the simplest if the levels allow it.

If the deeper floor of the new building puts its foundation level below the old one, the old footing has to be underpinned with concrete. This is a delicate operation: it is done in short sections that do not touch each other (1–3–5, then 2–4–6), so that the old wall is always supported.
Alternative: soil-concrete columns are formed under the old footing with jet grouting, taking its load down below the new foundation level – after that the excavation can be dug safely.
